8880.etyen:
Compound of Ciss (“C-sharp”) + dur (“major”), literally “C-sharp major”.
The first element Ciss (“C-sharp”) is the capitalized form of ciss, formed from c (“C”) and -iss (“sharp-note-forming suffix”). The suffix is from German -is (“sharp-note-forming suffix”), whose further origin is uncertain.
The second element dur (“major”) is via German Dur (“major”) from Middle High German bēdūre (“B-natural; hard B”), from Medieval Latin b durum (“hard B”). The adjective is from Latin dūrus (“hard”), from Proto-Italic *dūros (“hard”), from Proto-Indo-European *dweh₂rós (“long, far”), from the root *dweh

1000112.etyen:
Internationalism, based on English Zambia, the name adopted for the former Northern Rhodesia when the country became independent in 1964. The English name was formed from English Zambezi, the name of the river which flows through western Zambia and along much of its southern border.
The deeper origin of the river name Zambezi is uncertain. Store norske leksikon gives the interpretation “God's river”, but other historical explanations have also been proposed.
Compare the parallel international adaptations Norwegian Nynorsk Zambia, Danish Zambia, Swedish Zambia, German Sambia, French Zambie and

x: I fortellingen møter helten en mektig ifrit.
In the story, the hero meets a powerful ifrit.

1001392.etyen:
Borrowed from Arabic عِفْرِيت (ʕifrīt, “ifrit, powerful spirit or demon”), plural عَفَارِيت (ʕafārīt).
The Arabic word is traditionally connected by Arabic philologists with the root ع ف ر (ʕ f r), associated with senses such as “rebellious” and “strong”. In Islamic and Arabic folklore, the word came to denote a powerful, often hostile spirit or demon, commonly treated as a type of jinn (“jinn”).
Compare Danish ifrit, Swedish ifrit, German Ifrit, French ifrit and English ifrit.

1004720.etyen:
From Torje (“male given name”) + -sen (“patronymic suffix meaning “son of””), originally a patronymic meaning “son of Torje”. The given name Torje is a younger form related to Torjei and Torgeir, ultimately from Old Norse Þórgeirr, from Þórr (“Thor”) + geirr (“spear”).
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk Torjesen (“patronymic surname”).

en.g: Utoeya; an island in Tyrifjorden, in Hole municipality, Buskerud, Norway
x: AUF's summer camp is held on Utøya.
Det er nesten ikke til å fatte – kontrastene – hvor vakkert det er her på Utøya.

en.g: the massacre carried out on the island on 22 July 2011, the second of the two terrorist attacks carried out in Norway that day
x: Hun har skrevet om livet før og etter Utøya.
She has written about life before and after the Utøya massacre.
Utøya og 22. juli er ikke noe jeg tenker på daglig.
Utøya and 22 July are not things I think about every day.

1004976.etyen:
From utøy (“outer island”), the feminine definite singular form being utøya (“the outer island”). The noun is itself formed from ut (“out, outer”) + øy (“island”).
The name refers to the island's position as the outermost of the three islands Utøya, Geitøya and Storøya in this part of Tyrifjorden. Following the mass killing on the island on 22 July 2011, the place name also came to be used metonymically for the attack itself.
